questiontext.text:
Goal

A ferry operator needs counts for passenger crossings, scheduled sailings, and port-side seating. Complete each function using a different loop form.

Read
  • For statements. Find the subsections about a single condition and a for clause. When does Go evaluate the condition? Which semicolons can you omit?
  • For statements with range clause. Find the table row for an integer value and the paragraph beginning "For an integer value n". Which values does the loop produce for n? What happens when n is zero or negative?
Coming from Java

Java has four loop forms called for, while, do-while, and for-each. Go uses while for none of them. The content after for determines the loop form.

while (passengers > 0) { ... }
for (int hour = first; hour <= last; hour += every) { ... }
for (int ticket : tickets) { ... }
Required: for, range
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Find "only if the block was executed" in the for clause subsection. Trace a timetable whose last hour is before its first.
  • Find "If n <= 0" in the range subsection. Read that sentence and the preceding one.

Goal

The harbourmaster uses wind readings to describe conditions and decide whether a boat can sail. Complete the three functions using switches and an if with a short declaration.

Read
  • Switch statements. Read the Expression switches subsection and its examples. In what order does Go test case expressions? What happens after the matching clause runs? What does an omitted switch expression mean? In the first example, how does one clause match several values?
  • If statements. Read the last example. What can appear between if and its condition? Which branches can use the declared value?
Coming from Java

A Java switch continues into the next case unless the case ends with break. Java's arrow form prevents that fall-through. A Java developer might therefore end each clause with break or use an arrow.

switch (force) {
    case 3:
    case 6:
        System.out.println("breeze");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("unknown");
}
Banned: break
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Find "top-to-bottom" under Expression switches. Which clause wins when 2 knots satisfies more than one band?
  • Find the second example in that subsection. Read the comment beside the switch without an expression.

testcode.text: fmt.Println(force(-1), force(0), force(1), force(10), force(11)) fmt.Println(force(27), force(28), force(47), force(48)) fmt.Println(canSail(20, 6), canSail(20, 5))

questiontext.text:
Goal

At a ball, a matchmaker searches the tables for couples and awards consolation prizes. Complete the searches and check how many dance rounds fit the floor.

Read
  • Break statements. Which statements can a plain break leave? If those statements are nested, which one does break leave? In the example, what does the label change?
  • Continue statements. Read the first sentence and the sentence about labels. If the label names the outer loop, where does control continue?
  • Label scopes. Read the paragraph. How far does a label's scope extend? What happens if you declare a label but never use it?
Coming from Java

Java also has labelled break and continue, although many Java developers never use them. A common alternative sets a boolean flag in the inner loop and checks it in the outer loop. Java also permits labelling every loop before choosing a target.

boolean found = false;
for (int t = 1; t <= tables && !found; t++) {
    for (int s = 1; s <= seats; s++) {
        if (t * s == wish) { found = true; break; }
    }
}
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Find "innermost" under Break statements and consider how a search can leave both nested loops.
  • Find where a labelled continue resumes and consider when a table earns a consolation prize.
